intro.title: Your first program
intro.bodyMarkdown:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web: every website you use runs it in your browser, to make pages react when you click, type and scroll. It runs on servers and in apps too. Your browser already has JavaScript built in, so in CodeQuest your code runs right here, with nothing to install.

A JavaScript program is a list of instructions that run from top to bottom, one line at a time. You type code into the sandbox or a challenge, press **Run** or **Check**, and the browser runs it.

Your first instruction is `console.log()`. Whatever you put inside the brackets is shown as output. Text goes in quotes, so JavaScript knows it is text and not code. Numbers and maths don't need quotes.

```
console.log("Hello, world!")
console.log(42)
console.log(2 + 3)
```

Each `console.log()` writes one line. The quotes make all the difference: `console.log("2 + 3")` shows the text `2 + 3`, while `console.log(2 + 3)` works out the sum and shows `5`. You can give `console.log` several things separated by commas, and it shows them with a space between: `console.log("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3)` shows `2 + 3 = 5`.

Text can go in double quotes (`"Hi"`) or single quotes (`'Hi'`): both work, as long as the two ends match. CodeQuest mostly uses double quotes.

Lines that start with `//` are **comments**. JavaScript skips them; they are notes for the people who read the code. A comment can also go at the end of a line.

```
// Say hello
console.log("Hi!") // this line shows Hi!
```

Mistakes are normal, and JavaScript tells you about them. When it can't run your code, it stops and shows an **error**. `SyntaxError` means the code isn't written correctly, such as a missing bracket or quote. `ReferenceError: Console is not defined` means JavaScript doesn't know a name, usually because of a typo.

JavaScript is case-sensitive: `console.log` works, `Console.log` doesn't. Spelling matters exactly in the text you show too, because the challenges compare your output character by character.

You will often see lines that end with a semicolon, like `console.log("Hi");`. JavaScript adds them where they are missing, so they are optional here; CodeQuest leaves them out.

intro.title: Showing values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`console.log()` can show several values at once. Separate them with commas and it puts one space between each:

```
console.log("Apples:", 3, "Pears:", 5)
console.log(10, 20, 30)
```

Numbers can be whole (`7`), decimal (`2.5`) or negative (`-4`). JavaScript works out any maths before it shows the result, so `console.log(20 - 13.75)` shows `6.25`.

An empty `console.log()` shows an empty line, which is handy for spacing output out.

Text can hold the other kind of quote: `"It's sunny"` uses double quotes around a single quote, and `'She said "hi"'` the other way round.

A backslash starts an **escape**: a special character inside text. `\n` starts a new line, `\t` is a tab, `\"` is a double quote inside double quotes, and `\\` is one backslash.

```
console.log("Line one\nLine two")
console.log("Name\tScore")
console.log("She said \"hi\"")
```

Lines are shown in the order the code runs them, top to bottom. To change the order of the output, change the order of the lines.

intro.title: Variables: let and const
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **variable** is a name for a value, so you can use it again later. You make one with `const` or `let`, a name, `=` and the value:

```
const name = "Alex"
let score = 7
console.log(name, "has", score, "points")
```

Use the name without quotes: `console.log(name)` shows `Alex`, while `console.log("name")` shows the word `name`.

`const` is for a value that won't change. `let` is for one that will: you give it a new value with `=`, without writing `let` again.

```
let score = 7
score = 10
console.log(score)
```

A new value can use the old one: `score = score + 5` takes the current score, adds 5 and stores the result. Changing a `const` is a `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.`, which is the point of `const`: it protects values that should stay put. Start with `const`, and switch to `let` when a value needs to change.

Names can use letters, digits, `_` and `$`, but can't start with a digit or contain spaces. JavaScript names usually use **camelCase**: `totalPrice`, `firstName`. Names are case-sensitive, so `score` and `Score` are different variables.

Each name can be made once: a second `let score` is a `SyntaxError`. Using a variable before the line that makes it is a `ReferenceError`.

You may also see `var` in older code. It is the old way to make variables; `let` and `const` replace it.

intro.title: Numbers and arithmetic
intro.bodyMarkdown:
JavaScript has the usual maths operators: `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide, and two more: `%` gives the **remainder** after dividing, and `**` raises to a power.

```
console.log(7 + 2, 7 - 2, 7 * 2, 7 / 2)
console.log(7 % 2, 2 ** 3)
```

Whole numbers and decimals are the same kind of value, a `number`, so `7 / 2` is simply `3.5`. Dividing by zero doesn't stop the program: it gives `Infinity`.

`%` is useful more often than it looks: `n % 2` is `0` for even numbers and `1` for odd ones, and `125 % 60` is the minutes left over after taking out whole hours.

As in maths, `*`, `/` and `%` are worked out before `+` and `-`, and `**` before all of them. Brackets change the order: `2 + 3 * 4` is `14`, but `(2 + 3) * 4` is `20`.

Shortcuts change a variable using its own value: `score += 5` means `score = score + 5`, and there are `-=`, `*=` and `/=` too. `count++` adds 1 and `count--` takes 1 away.

```
let score = 10
score += 5
score *= 2
let count = 0
count++
console.log(score, count)
```

Computers store decimals in binary, so a few of them can't be stored exactly: `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. That is normal in every language. When it matters (money, for example), round the result, as the Math stage shows.

intro.title: Math: rounding and more
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`Math` is a built-in toolbox of maths functions. You use each one as `Math.` and its name, with the number in brackets.

```
console.log(Math.round(4.6), Math.floor(4.6), Math.ceil(4.2))
console.log(Math.max(3, 9, 5), Math.min(3, 9, 5))
console.log(Math.abs(-7), Math.sqrt(81))
```

There are three ways to round to a whole number. `Math.round` goes to the nearest (`4.5` becomes `5`), `Math.floor` always goes down, and `Math.ceil` always goes up. `Math.trunc` simply cuts off the decimals.

`Math.max` and `Math.min` take any number of values and give the largest or smallest. `Math.abs` gives the distance from zero, so it turns `-7` into `7`. `Math.sqrt` is the square root, and `Math.PI` is π.

To round to 2 decimal places for showing, use a number's `toFixed(2)`: `(4.567).toFixed(2)` gives `"4.57"`. It gives **text**, which is right for showing a price but not for more maths.

```
const price = 19.999
console.log(price.toFixed(2))
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2))
```

To round and keep a number, scale up, round and scale back: `Math.round(price * 100) / 100`.

`Math.random()` gives a different decimal between 0 and 1 each time, which games use for dice and shuffling. Because its answer changes, the challenges here don't use it.

intro.title: Strings: working with text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A piece of text is called a **string**. `+` joins strings together; this is called **concatenation**. It adds no spaces of its own, so put them in the text where you want them:

```
const first = "Ada"
const last = "Lovelace"
const full = first + " " + last
console.log(full)
```

`+=` adds to the end of a string you already have: `message += "!"`.

Every string has a `length`: how many characters it has, counting spaces and punctuation. `"Hello".length` is `5`. It has no brackets, because it is a value the string carries, not something it does.

Each character has a position, its **index**, counting from **0**. `word[0]` is the first character, and the last one is `word[word.length - 1]`, because a 5-letter word's indexes go from 0 to 4. `word.at(-1)` is a shortcut for the last character.

```
const word = "Hello"
console.log(word.length, word[0], word[4], word.at(-1))
```

An index past the end gives `undefined`, JavaScript's value for "nothing here".

Strings can't be changed in place: `word[0] = "J"` does nothing. To change a string you build a new one, such as `"J" + word.slice(1)` (you will meet `slice` in the string methods stage).

intro.title: Template literals
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Joining text with `+` gets fiddly: quotes, plus signs and spaces everywhere. A **template literal** is easier. It is text in backticks (`` ` ``, usually at the top left of the keyboard), and `${…}` drops a value straight into it:

```
const name = "Sam"
const age = 12
console.log(`${name} is ${age} years old`)
```

Inside `${…}` you can put any expression, not just a variable: `${price * 2}`, `${name.length}` or `${Math.round(score)}` are worked out first, then put in the text.

```
const price = 4.5
const count = 3
console.log(`${count} items cost ${price * count}`)
console.log(`Total: $${(price * count).toFixed(2)}`)
```

The `$` before `{` is what marks the gap. A `$` on its own, as in `$13.50`, is just a character, so `$${total}` shows a dollar sign and then the value.

A template literal can also go over several lines: the line breaks inside the backticks are kept. And both kinds of quote can go inside one without escapes: `` `It's "fine"` ``.

```
const poem = `Roses are red,
Violets are blue.`
console.log(poem)
```

Only backticks do this. In `"Hi ${name}"`, with ordinary quotes, `${name}` is just shown as it is.

intro.title: String methods
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Strings come with **methods**: things a string can do, written after a dot with brackets. Each gives back a **new** string (or another value) and leaves the original as it was.

```
const name = "  ada Lovelace  "
console.log(name.trim())
console.log(name.toUpperCase())
console.log(name.toLowerCase())
```

`trim()` removes spaces from both ends. `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` change the letters. Methods can be chained, one after another: `name.trim().toUpperCase()`.

`includes("x")` tells you whether some text appears (`true` or `false`), and `startsWith` and `endsWith` check the two ends. `indexOf("x")` gives where it first appears, or `-1` if it doesn't.

`slice(start, end)` cuts out a part: from index `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Leave out `end` to go to the end, and use a negative number to count from the end: `slice(-4)` is the last 4 characters.

```
const word = "JavaScript"
console.log(word.slice(0, 4), word.slice(4), word.slice(-6))
console.log(word.includes("Script"), word.indexOf("S"))
```

`replace(a, b)` swaps the first `a` for `b`, and `replaceAll` swaps every one. `repeat(n)` repeats a string, and `padStart(length, fill)` adds fill at the start until the string is that long, which is handy for lining up numbers: `"7".padStart(3, "0")` is `"007"`.

Because strings never change, a method on its own does nothing you can see: `name.trim()` gives a trimmed copy, so store it (`const clean = name.trim()`) or show it.

intro.title: Types and conversion
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every value has a **type**. So far you have met `number` (`7`, `2.5`), `string` (`"hi"`) and, in the next stage, `boolean` (`true` or `false`). `undefined` means "no value yet". `typeof` tells you a value's type, as text:

```
console.log(typeof 42, typeof "42", typeof true, typeof undefined)
```

`42` and `"42"` look alike but are different: one is a number, the other is text. Text that comes from outside a program, such as what someone types into a form, is always a string, even when it is digits.

That matters with `+`. If either side is a string, `+` joins instead of adding: `"5" + 3` is `"53"`. The other maths operators only work on numbers, so they turn the text into a number first: `"5" * 3` is `15` and `"5" - 3` is `2`. Relying on that is confusing, so convert on purpose.

```
console.log("5" + 3, "5" * 3, "5" - 3)
console.log(Number("5") + 3)
```

`Number(text)` turns text into a number. `parseInt(text)` and `parseFloat(text)` read a number from the start of text and stop at the first character that doesn't fit, so `parseInt("12px")` is `12`; `parseInt` also drops any decimals. `String(value)` turns a value into text.

When text isn't a number at all, the result is `NaN`, "Not a Number": `Number("hello")` is `NaN`. Any maths with `NaN` gives `NaN` again, so check with `Number.isNaN(value)`. Oddly, `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.

```
console.log(Number("hello"), parseInt("12px"), parseFloat("3.75kg"))
console.log(Number.isNaN(Number("abc")))
```

intro.title: True or false: comparing values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **boolean** is one of two values, `true` or `false`. You get one whenever you compare two values:

```
const age = 14
console.log(age > 12, age < 10, age >= 14, age <= 13)
```

`>` and `<` are greater and less than, and `>=` and `<=` include equal. `===` asks whether two values are the same, and `!==` whether they are different. A single `=` is not a comparison: it gives a variable a value.

```
const password = "open-sesame"
console.log(password === "open-sesame", password !== "letmein")
```

`===` is strict: the type has to match too, so `5 === "5"` is `false` (a number isn't a string). There is also a loose `==` that converts types first, so `5 == "5"` is `true`, along with surprises like `0 == ""`. Always use `===` and `!==`.

Strings compare letter by letter and are case-sensitive: `"cat" === "Cat"` is `false`. To compare without caring about case, change both first: `a.toLowerCase() === b.toLowerCase()`.

Booleans can be stored and combined. `&&` (and) is true only when both sides are true; `||` (or) is true when at least one is; `!` (not) turns one around.

```
const age = 15
const hasTicket = true
const canEnter = age >= 12 && hasTicket
console.log(canEnter, !canEnter, age < 12 || hasTicket)
```

In the next quest, these true-or-false values decide what a program does, with `if` and loops.
